transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-12-15
Start time: 14:30 PST
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Rajiv Patel (CISO - Silverline), Elena Ruiz (Head of Cloud Arch), Marcus Lee (Security Engineer)

Summary:
Brief security review focused on encryption at rest/in transit, KMS options (CMEK, BYOK), HSM-backed keys, attestation, key rotation and operational impact. Customer wants to validate Redwood's private deployment and BYOK story for regulated workloads; ask for artifacts and architecture diagram plus perf numbers for HSM latency.

Topics Covered:
- Encryption in transit (TLS, mTLS)
- Encryption at rest (disk, DB, object storage)
- Envelope encryption + customer-managed keys (CMEK)
- BYOK options and HSM integration (Cloud HSM vs on-prem HSM)
- Key rotation and audit/logging (KMS access logs, audit trail retention)
- Compliance artifacts (SOC 2, ISO 27001)
- Performance overhead and fallback modes for dedicated/private ramps

[00:00] Maya Chen: All right, hey everyone thanks for joining, um this is Maya from Redwood, with Liam our solutions engineer. Quick intro and then we can jump into your questions on encryption and KMS.
[00:10] Rajiv Patel: Thanks Maya, yeah I'm Rajiv, CISO at Silverline. We, uh, we run core banking workloads and encryption at rest is obviously table stakes. We're specifically trying to understand how Redwood supports customer-managed keys and whether an HSM-backed key store is possible.
[00:25] Liam O'Connor: Yep, great. At a high level we support envelope encryption for data at rest where the data keys are wrapped by a customer-managed key in your KMS provider. That can be AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS, Azure Key Vault, or an on-prem HSM via our private deployment.
[00:42] Elena Ruiz: When you say envelope encryption, can you show where the key material lives and how Redwood's runtime touches it? We need to map it to our architecture diagram for auditors.
[00:55] Liam O'Connor: Sure, so typical flow: application request -> Redwood ingress -> runtime generates a per-object or per-request data key (DEK) locally, encrypts the payload with the DEK, then calls your KMS to wrap the DEK with your CMK. The wrapped DEK is stored alongside the ciphertext. On decrypt, the runtime calls KMS to unwrap the DEK and then decrypts locally. That means your CMK never leaves your KMS and Redwood only holds wrapped keys.
[01:20] Marcus Lee: How does that work with KV cache? Our concern is that the KV cache holds unencrypted model state during a session — do you encrypt the cache or is the cache ephemeral and in RAM only?
[01:35] Liam O'Connor: Good question. The KV cache in our serving runtime is memory-resident; it's not persisted to disk by default. On private deployments we can configure persistent caches — if you enable persistence we use envelope encryption to encrypt on-disk cache blobs. For hosted we keep the cache RAM-only and it's ephemeral per instance, and we rotate instances. There's a few nuances around snapshots and warm starts which we'll show on the diagram.
[01:58] Rajiv Patel: Ok, is that certified FIPS/HSM workflow? Our auditors ask about FIPS 140-2 validated HSM and hardware attestation.
[02:08] Liam O'Connor: For HSM-backed keys we integrate with cloud HSM offerings which are FIPS 140-2/140-3 validated (e.g., AWS CloudHSM). For on-prem HSMs in our Private deployment, we support Luna/Thales or other PKCS#11-compatible devices; attestation and key import flows are supported via standard BYOK procedures. We can provide our HSM integration appendix.
[02:32] Elena Ruiz: Do you support split knowledge or split custody (i.e., dual control) for key creation/imports?
[02:40] Maya Chen: Short answer: yes. Our recommended enterprise pattern is that customers use their own KMS which enforces dual control policies. Redwood never has unwrapped key material. For on-prem import we recommend hardware-backed key import with admin approval steps. We'll include those details in the artifact pack.
[02:56] Marcus Lee: What's the runtime overhead when you call KMS for unwrap on every session start? Could that add latency to our 100ms SLO?
[03:05] Liam O'Connor: We try to minimize KMS round trips by doing local DEK caching for active sessions and by using envelope encryption so we avoid calling KMS for every token. Typically the unwrap is done once per session or per model shard activation. For HSM-backed CMEK there is additional latency — we see unwrap times in the 10-50ms range depending on provider and region; we'll provide measured numbers for your region.
[03:30] Rajiv Patel: So if we do a private deployment in our VPC with our KMS, would Redwood ever require outbound network to any third-party KMS? We need to ensure keys never leave our control.
[03:41] Maya Chen: For private on-prem or VPC deployments you can point Redwood to your KMS endpoint. There is no requirement to route keys to Redwood-managed cloud. Wrapped DEKs are what may transit if you choose Redwood-hosted storage, but the CMK and unwrapped key material remain in your KMS. If you want total isolation we also offer an on-prem package where metadata and blobs are in your environment.
[04:00] Elena Ruiz: Audit logging — does Redwood emit KMS access logs or its own audit trail for key usage? We need key usage logs for our audit.
[04:09] Liam O'Connor: Two parts: your KMS will have its own access logs (e.g., CloudTrail for AWS) showing Encrypt/Decrypt/GenerateDataKey calls. Separately Redwood emits audit logs for higher-level operations (deployment changes, config changes, who triggered key wraps) which can be shipped to your SIEM or S3 bucket. We can configure retention windows per your compliance needs.
[04:30] Rajiv Patel: Retention length? Our policy is seven years for some artifacts.
[04:36] Maya Chen: We can support long-term retention for audit artifacts as an add-on. For hosted customers we have tiered retention; for dedicated/private you control retention in your storage. We'll include the retention options in the docs.
[04:50] Marcus Lee: What about key rotation? If we rotate CMKs, how do you handle wrapped DEKs? Do you rewrap existing ciphertext?
[04:59] Liam O'Connor: We support lazy rewrap and on-access rewrap. When a CMK rotates you can either rewrap existing wrapped DEKs in bulk via a rewrap job or on decrypt we unwrap with the old key and rewrap with the new CMK. We provide a rewrap utility and automation we can run with your approval.
[05:18] Elena Ruiz: For BYOK, we prefer to import keys rather than create keys in the cloud KMS. Is Redwood okay with imported keys?
[05:25] Liam O'Connor: Yes. Imported keys or externally generated keys (with proper key material import) are supported as long as the KMS supports wrap/unwrap APIs. For HSM-backed imported keys we can document the import/attestation steps.
[05:38] Rajiv Patel: Any regulatory gotchas for data residency? We have European customers so some PII must remain in-region.
[05:45] Maya Chen: You can pin model routing and storage to regions. For hosted we have region-aware deployment; for dedicated and private you can select region or keep on-prem. We'll include region pinning and data residency configurations.
[05:58] Marcus Lee: Can you share an example policy for least privilege access to the CMK for Redwood's runtime? We need a template for the auditors.
[06:06] Liam O'Connor: Absolutely — we have example IAM/KMS policies that grant Encrypt/Decrypt/GenerateDataKey only to the Redwood service principal, scoped to resource ARNs and with conditions like VPC endpoint or source IP. We'll attach that.
[06:20] Rajiv Patel: Are there known failure modes where KMS outages would take down inference? What's your recommended fallback?
[06:27] Maya Chen: We recommend: 1) local DEK cache to allow short-term operations during KMS transient errors, 2) automatic degraded mode using a fallback key under customer policy (with approval), and 3) rate-limit retries with exponential backoff. For critical workloads we recommend Dedicated with multi-region KMS failover. We'll show our SLA and suggested patterns.
[06:50] Elena Ruiz: For attestation, do you provide HSM audit logs and attestation artifacts?
[06:56] Liam O'Connor: We can provide HSM attestation reports for cloud HSM providers and integration docs for on-prem HSMs. The attestation flow depends on the HSM vendor; we'll include vendor-specific guides.
[07:08] Marcus Lee: What about encryption in transit between our VPC and Redwood control plane or between subcomponents? Is mTLS enforced end-to-end?
[07:16] Maya Chen: Yes. We enforce TLS 1.2+ and mTLS for control plane connections; customer-data plane traffic in private deployments can be configured to use mutual TLS and pinned certs. For hosted we use TLS with strict cipher suites and we rotate certs regularly.
[07:33] Rajiv Patel: Is there any place where plaintext might be logged accidentally? For example, request/response bodies in debug logs?
[07:40] Liam O'Connor: We scrub PII and request bodies from debug logs by default, but we also give customers a toggle for redaction levels. For compliance-sensitive deployments we set redaction to max and only log metadata. We'll document our redaction rules and offer options for full scrubbing.
[07:58] Elena Ruiz: Okay, last bit: can you summarize the artifacts you'll send?
[08:02] Maya Chen: Sure. We'll send: SOC 2 Type II report, ISO 27001 summary, KMS/HSM integration appendix, envelope encryption architecture diagram, IAM/KMS policy templates, audit log retention options, and measured latency numbers for HSM unwrap in your region.
[08:20] Marcus Lee: Great. Also please include a short write-up on how the runtime caches DEKs and when it will call KMS — auditors like to see concrete TTL values.
[08:30] Liam O'Connor: We'll include TTL defaults and config knobs; by default DEK cache TTL is configurable, default 15 minutes for session caches, and we provide a control to set to 0 to force unwrap per request.
[08:45] Rajiv Patel: Can we get a short runbook for key compromise — steps to rotate and rewrap, revoke access, and forensic logs?
[08:53] Maya Chen: Yes we'll include an incident response runbook tailored to BYOK/HSM scenarios.

-- Transcript drops / small crosstalk and filler bits omitted for brevity --

[22:11] Liam O'Connor: Quick live note — if you opt for on-prem HSM we'll need a network diagram and the PKCS#11 endpoint details; also target firmware version for the vendor.
[22:23] Elena Ruiz: Got it, we'll pull that from our infra team and send to Marcus.
[22:29] Marcus Lee: I'll collect the KMS ARNs and rotation schedules and drop into the CRM/secure share.

[33:02] Rajiv Patel: One more security question — do you support customer-provided HSM attestation for every key import or only initial?
[33:11] Liam O'Connor: We can do per-import attestation if your process requires it. It is, however, more operationally heavy. We'll propose two modes in the doc: per-import attestation and bulk import with sampled attestation.

[40:05] Maya Chen: Alright, quick recap and next steps: we'll send the compliance pack and architecture diagrams by tomorrow, Liam will prepare the envelope encryption diagram and latency numbers, Marcus will share KMS details. We'll schedule a follow-up technical deep dive with your DevOps next week.
[40:22] Rajiv Patel: That works, thanks everyone.
[40:26] Elena Ruiz: Thanks, appreciate the detail.
[40:29] Marcus Lee: Thanks, talk soon.
